nodes.text: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
nodes.teacher: Express length as a whole number of length units

nodes.text: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.
nodes.teacher: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole
nodes.reteach: Stress 'the same whole'. Half a small pizza and half a large one is where this breaks.

nodes.text: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.
nodes.kid: Shapes stay the same when you turn them
nodes.teacher: Name shapes regardless of orientation or size

nodes.text: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
nodes.kid: What the equals sign really means
nodes.teacher: Meaning of the equal sign

nodes.text: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.
nodes.teacher: Rectangular arrays and repeated addition

nodes.text: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
nodes.teacher: Compose simple shapes into larger shapes

nodes.text: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.
nodes.teacher: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares; describe using halves and fourths
nodes.reteach: Vocabulary plus fair-sharing language: 'would that be fair?' is the most reliable prompt at this age.

nodes.text: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
nodes.teacher: Fluency within 20

nodes.text: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.
nodes.kid: Fractions that look different but are worth the same
nodes.teacher: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size
nodes.reteach: Same-size wholes, different cuts, side by side. Comparison is meaningless if the wholes differ.

nodes.text: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.
nodes.kid: Putting things in order by length
nodes.teacher: Order three objects by length; compare indirectly

nodes.text: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.
nodes.teacher: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools
nodes.reteach: Watch for starting at 1 instead of 0.

nodes.text: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
nodes.kid: Fraction word problems where the bottoms match
nodes.teacher: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators
nodes.reteach: Keep the denominator fixed and vary the story. Isolates the language from the arithmetic.

nodes.text: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.
nodes.teacher: Successive number names increase by one

nodes.text: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.
nodes.kid: Why 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount
nodes.teacher: Explain why a/b is equivalent to (n x a)/(n x b) using visual fraction models
nodes.reteach: Fold the same strip twice. The amount did not change, only the number of cuts. Students who 'know' equivalence often think the fraction got bigger.

nodes.text: Fluently add and subtract within 5.
nodes.kid: Adding and taking away up to 5
nodes.teacher: Fluently add and subtract within 5

nodes.text: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, "flat") or three-dimensional ("solid").
nodes.teacher: Two-dimensional versus three-dimensional

nodes.text: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
nodes.kid: Building shapes out of other shapes
nodes.teacher: Compose 2-D shapes

nodes.text: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.
nodes.teacher: Subtract multiples of 10 within 10-90

nodes.text: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).
nodes.teacher: Relate counting to addition and subtraction

nodes.text: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
nodes.kid: Splitting a rectangle into equal squares
nodes.teacher: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count them
nodes.reteach: Links partitioning to area and later to multiplication.

nodes.text: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:
nodes.teacher: Two-digit numbers as tens and ones

nodes.text: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.
nodes.teacher: Count to 120 from any starting number

nodes.text: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
nodes.kid: Breaking a fraction into smaller pieces
nodes.teacher: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator
nodes.reteach: 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4, with a bar model beside it. Decomposition is what makes addition make sense later.

nodes.text: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
nodes.teacher: Add and subtract within 100 in word problems

nodes.text: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.
nodes.kid: Measuring the same thing with different rulers
nodes.teacher: Measure the length of an object twice using different length units; describe how the measurements relate
nodes.reteach: Bigger unit, smaller number. This inverse relationship IS the denominator idea, three years early, and almost nobody connects the two.

nodes.text: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.
nodes.kid: Finding fractions on a number line
nodes.teacher: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line
nodes.reteach: The jump from 'fraction as shaded pizza' to 'fraction as a number' is a real conceptual leap. Number lines are where fractions stop being pictures.

nodes.text: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.
nodes.kid: Adding and taking away up to 10
nodes.teacher: Solve word problems within 10

nodes.text: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
nodes.teacher: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators

nodes.text: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1).
nodes.teacher: Decompose numbers up to 10 in more than one way

nodes.text: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
nodes.teacher: Multiplication and division word problems within 100

nodes.text: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.
nodes.teacher: Multiplicative comparison word problems

nodes.text: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.
nodes.kid: What you can measure about something
nodes.teacher: Describe measurable attributes

nodes.text: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, thirds, half of, a third of, etc., and describe the whole as two halves, three thirds, four fourths. Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.
nodes.teacher: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares
nodes.reteach: Physical folding, not worksheets. This is where 'equal' first has to mean equal.

nodes.text: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
nodes.teacher: Count to 100 by ones and tens

nodes.text: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.
nodes.teacher: Estimate lengths using standard units

nodes.text: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.
nodes.teacher: Interpret whole-number quotients

nodes.text: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
nodes.teacher: Determine the unknown in an equation

nodes.text: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2, …, and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram.
nodes.teacher: Whole numbers as lengths on a number line

nodes.text: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
nodes.teacher: Odd and even numbers up to 20

nodes.text: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
nodes.teacher: Word problems within 20

nodes.text: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
nodes.teacher: Interpret products of whole numbers as equal groups
nodes.reteach: 5 x 7 as five groups of seven. Equal groups is the same idea as equal parts, in a different costume.

nodes.text: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.
nodes.teacher: Mentally find 10 more or 10 less

nodes.text: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 18 = 10 + 8); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
nodes.teacher: Compose and decompose 11-19 as ten and ones

nodes.text: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
nodes.teacher: Represent addition and subtraction

nodes.text: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
nodes.teacher: Properties of operations as strategies

nodes.text: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
nodes.teacher: Subtraction as an unknown-addend problem

nodes.text: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.
nodes.kid: Cutting a whole into equal parts
nodes.teacher: Understand a fraction 1/b as one part when a whole is partitioned into b EQUAL parts
nodes.reteach: Show a shape cut into 4 unequal pieces and ask if the shaded one is a quarter. The word 'equal' is doing all the work in this standard and is the single most-skipped idea in elementary fractions.

nodes.text: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.
nodes.teacher: Add within 100 using place value

nodes.text: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of"/"less of" the attribute, and describe the difference.
nodes.teacher: Directly compare two objects by a shared attribute

nodes.text: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
nodes.teacher: Describe shapes and relative positions

nodes.text: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.
nodes.teacher: Find the number that makes 10

nodes.text: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
nodes.kid: Adding fractions with different bottom numbers
nodes.teacher: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators
nodes.reteach: Before any common-denominator procedure, check they can say WHY fourths and sixths cannot be counted together. Most who fail here can execute the algorithm but cannot explain it.
